edges.effect_quant: Across prospective ICU cohorts, longer delirium duration consistently predicts worse cognition months later. In the original ventilated-medical-ICU cohort, 79% of survivors were cognitively impaired at 3 months and 71% at 12 months, with delirium duration independently predicting worse scores. In BRAIN-ICU and related analyses, three versus zero days of sedative-associated delirium predicted a 4.03-point lower RBANS global cognition score at 12 months, and longer hypoactive delirium was associated with 5.13-point lower global cognition at 3 months.
edges.population: adult survivors of critical illness, especially ICU patients with shock or respiratory failure who experienced delirium during hospitalization
edges.mechanism: ICU delirium likely marks and contributes to acute brain injury through neuroinflammation, disturbed neurotransmission, hypoxemia, sepsis, sleep disruption, and sedative toxicity. Longer delirium exposure may therefore reduce cognitive reserve and leave persistent deficits in memory, attention, and executive function long after the acute illness resolves.
edges.summary: This is one of the clearer harmful neurocognitive signals in critical care. Multiple prospective cohorts, including BRAIN-ICU, show that longer ICU delirium is associated with worse cognitive outcomes months later, and the association remains after adjustment for baseline vulnerability and illness severity.
edges.caveats: The evidence is observational, so delirium may partly be a marker of overall acute brain injury rather than the sole cause of later decline. Even so, the consistency across cohorts and delirium phenotypes makes it hard to dismiss as pure confounding, particularly because modifiable exposures such as sedation appear to matter.
